summary: Describes data types and algorithms that make it easier and safer to define and handle HTTP header and trailer fields, known as Structured Fields. It is meant for specifications of new HTTP fields. It obsoletes RFC 8941.

eli5.summary: HTTP messages carry little notes called headers. This sets one clear way to write the notes so every program reads them the same, rather than each note having its own odd style.

questions: how to parse structured field values
how are structured field values parsed
what types do structured fields support
subtitle: A common data model and strict parser for new HTTP header and trailer fields: lists, dictionaries and typed items.

tldr.problem: Each new HTTP field tends to invent its own slightly different syntax, so authors face many pitfalls and implementers must write a bespoke parser and serializer for each one.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three top-level types (List, Dictionary, Item) built from Integers, Decimals, Strings, Tokens, Byte Sequences, Booleans, Dates and Display Strings, plus step-by-step parsing and serialization algorithms that fail the whole field on any error.
tldr.outcome: New fields can opt in and share one generic implementation. This RFC adds Date and Display String and obsoletes RFC 8941.

today: RFC 9651 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2024. It obsoletes RFC 8941, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Structured Fields Exist
sections.content:
Specifying the syntax of a new HTTP header or trailer field is onerous, and once it is defined, bespoke parsers and serializers often have to be written because every field handles what looks like common syntax slightly differently. This RFC introduces common data structures for field definitions: an abstract model plus a concrete serialization for HTTP header and trailer fields.

It is not a goal to redefine the syntax of existing fields. Only fields that explicitly opt in use it, and future versions of HTTP can define alternative serializations of the same abstract model.

Strict processing is deliberate. The only error handling defined is to fail the entire operation, because a tolerant parser would pressure other implementations into similar but subtly different workarounds.
sections.eli5: Instead of everyone inventing their own way to write a note, there is one rulebook. If a note breaks the rules, it is ignored rather than guessed at.

sections.title: Defining a New Structured Field
sections.content:
To make a field a Structured Field, its authors normatively reference the RFC, say whether it is a header, a trailer or both, pick the top-level type (List, Dictionary or Item), define the semantics, and add any constraints. A definition applies to the entire field value, not a portion of it.

When parsing fails, the entire field is ignored, and definitions cannot override that, though they can add constraints. Violating a field-specific constraint also means the whole field is ignored, unless the definition says otherwise.

For extensibility, fields must be an Item, List or Dictionary, since Items and Inner Lists can carry Parameters. Authors are discouraged from treating an unknown parameter as an error, and may ask senders to add grease parameters so recipients do not write parsers that skip Parameters. A field that references RFC 8941 cannot use the newer Date type, because older parsers would reject it, although this RFC's parser can still parse valid fields that reference RFC 8941.
sections.eli5: Anyone who invents a new note type says which shape it is and what the rules are. Extra unknown add-ons should be politely ignored so the note can grow later.

sections.title: Lists, Dictionaries and Parameters
sections.content:
A List is an array of zero or more members, each an Item or an Inner List. On the wire members are separated by commas, as in Example-List: sugar, tea, rum, and a List can be split across multiple lines of the same section, though a single member cannot. An empty List or Dictionary is represented by not sending the field.

An Inner List is written in parentheses with space-separated Items, for example ("foo" "bar"). A Dictionary is an ordered map of unique, lowercase keys to Items or Inner Lists, written as key=value pairs separated by commas. Recipients MUST ignore members whose keys are unknown, unless the field's specification disallows them.

Parameters are ordered key-value pairs attached to an Item or Inner List with semicolons, and keys cannot contain uppercase letters. A Boolean true value in a Dictionary member or Parameter MUST be omitted when serializing, so a=?0, b, c; foo=bar has b and c as true.

Parsers MUST support at least 1024 members in a List or Dictionary, 256 members in an Inner List, 256 parameters on an Item or Inner List, and keys of at least 64 characters.
sections.eli5: A list is a row of things, a dictionary is a set of labeled boxes, and parameters are little sticky notes on a thing. Everything keeps the order it was written in.

sections.title: The Item Types
sections.content:
An Item is one of eight types. Integers run from -999,999,999,999,999 to 999,999,999,999,999 (up to fifteen digits), for IEEE 754 compatibility. Decimals have at most 12 integer digits and at most three fractional digits. Strings are printable ASCII (%x20 to %x7E) in double quotes, where only the double quote and backslash can be escaped.

Tokens start with an alphabetic character or an asterisk, and are short textual words; new fields are encouraged to use Strings instead. Byte Sequences are base64 between colons. Booleans are ?1 or ?0. Dates are an @ followed by seconds from 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, excluding leap seconds.

Display Strings allow Unicode scalar values by percent-encoding non-ASCII characters after a leading %. They are NOT RECOMMENDED where a String or Token would do, since Unicode brings normalization and homograph concerns.

Parsers MUST support Strings of at least 1024 characters, Tokens of at least 512 characters and Byte Sequences of at least 16384 octets after decoding.
sections.eli5: Each value is one of a few kinds: a whole number, a number with a decimal point, some plain text, a short word, a blob of bytes, a yes or no, a date, or fancy text that can hold any language.

sections.title: Serializing and Parsing
sections.content:
Section 4 gives step-by-step algorithms. Serialization returns an ASCII string for the field value. Lists and Dictionaries put a comma and a single space between members, and Inner Lists use a single space between Items. Implementations MAY vary from the serialization algorithm as long as the output is correctly handled by the parser.

Parsing is mandatory to follow: behavior MUST be indistinguishable from the algorithm. A parser discards leading spaces, parses a List, Dictionary or Item according to the field's declared type, discards leading spaces again, and fails if any input is left over. Before parsing, it MUST combine all field lines in the same section with a matching name into one comma-separated value.

That combining is why members of Lists and Dictionaries can be split across lines, but Strings split across lines give unpredictable results and Tokens, Integers, Decimals and Byte Sequences cannot be split at all, because the inserted commas make parsing fail.
sections.eli5: There is a recipe for writing a note and a recipe for reading it. The reader follows the recipe exactly, and if anything is left over or looks wrong, the whole note is tossed out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Most types have no size limit, so extremely large fields could be an attack vector, for example for resource consumption. Most HTTP implementations limit the size of individual fields and of the whole header or trailer section to mitigate this.

Parties able to inject new HTTP fields can change the meaning of a Structured Field. In some circumstances parsing will fail, but it cannot reliably fail in all of them.

Display Strings can carry any Unicode code point without sanitization, including unassigned code points, control points (including NUL) and noncharacters. Applications should consider filtering or escaping untrusted content before displaying it.
sections.eli5: Someone could send a gigantic note to hog the reader, or sneak in an extra line to change what a note means. And fancy text can hide odd characters, so check it before showing it to people.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 8941
sections.content:
This revision adds the Date type and the Display String type, and moves the ABNF to an informative appendix, no longer encouraging ABNF in definitions of new Structured Fields. It refines parse failure handling.

It also adds a "Structured Type" column to the HTTP Field Name Registry and fills it in for existing entries such as Accept-CH (List), CDN-Cache-Control (Dictionary) and Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy (Item). Appendix A explains why JSON was not used: it has issues with large numbers, duplicate members, Unicode strings and unbounded nesting.
sections.eli5: The new edition added two more kinds of value, dates and fancy text, and tidied up some wording and lists.
